utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. This is a preliminary conference in the matter of the Prosecutor of the Tribunal versus Dusan Tadic, case number IT 94-1-T. I see a lot of lawyers over there. There are a lot of lawyers here. First would you please tell me who is appearing for the Prosecutor today?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honour pleases, to my right is Miss Hollis. I appear. My name is Mr Niemann. To my left ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I did not hear you, Mr Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, to my right is Miss Hollis. I am appearing, my name is Niemann. To my immediate left is Mr Tieger. Next to him is Mr Keegan, and next to him is Mr Fenrick.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Judge Deschênes wants you to speak these names slowly so he can write them down. Spell the last name for me, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: F-e-n-r-i-c-k.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DESCHENES
utterances.text: Mr Fenrick, of course. I missed the previous name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I will spell them all. Miss Hollis, H-o-l-l-i-s, my name is spelt N-i-e-m-a-n-n. Mr Tieger, spelt T-i-e-g-e-r and Mr Keegan, spelt K-e-e-g-a-n.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DESCHENES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Then of course Mr Fenrick, which you have spelt twice. Is it still spelt F-e-n-r-i-c-k, is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Fine, thank you very much. Who is appearing, please, for the accused? PROFESSOR WLADIMIROFF: If your Honour pleases, my name is Wladimiroff. To my left is present Mr van Sasse van Ysselt. I have given the name to the lady who is taking notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: To your immediate left is Mr Vujin. PROFESSOR WLADIMIROFF: I am starting at the end. I am working down to myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Go ahead. PROFESSOR WLADIMIROFF: Mr van Sasse van Ysselt. Next to him Mr Simic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: The Judges want to get the names spelt. Would you spell that young man's name for me, please? PROFESSOR WLADIMIROFF: v-a-n S-a-s-s-e, then separately v-a-n Y-s-s-e-l-t. It is pronounced "van Sasse van Ysselt".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: In any case he, I gather, is one of your legal assistants. In a moment I will tell you about the role of legal assistants. Since they will not be participating, I do not think that I will have to address him; therefore I do not really need to know, with all due respect. PROFESSOR WLADIMIROFF: Yes, I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: The next gentleman? PROFESSOR WLADIMIROFF: Mr Simic from Banja Luko. Next to me is Mr Vujin, and on the other side to my right starting at the end of the bar table Miss Gilzing, G-i-l-z-i-n-g. I have also passed that name to the lady who takes notes, and next to me Miss Boot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Very good. Thank you, Mr Wladimiroff. This is a preliminary conference. You may recall that in our last meeting I indicated that we would be meeting again to discuss preliminary matters. I expect it to be a rather informal meeting. I guess, however, we cannot do in this Tribunal too many things informally, but I did want us to really meet to talk about the filing of preliminary motions. First, as kind of a housekeeping measure, I want to make sure that everyone who is listening to me through their earphones can hear the interpreter translating in the language that you speak. Mr Simic, I see you with earphones on. Can you hear the interpreter? She is translating for you, and I see Mr Tadic with earphones on. Can you hear me, Mr Tadic, in the language that you speak, of course? You can? Okay, very good. Let me outline, if I may, a few preliminary matters regarding these motions that we are going to talk about today. The first thing I want to do today is to hear from counsel regarding their intentions as to the preliminary motions, and pre-trial motions, that you may be filing. However, before we even begin that, let me give you a few guidelines, so to speak, about these motions. You may recall that, when we last met, I suggested that we have kind of a standard response period. Our Rules of Procedure and Evidence do not set out a specific period of time, in which a party would have to respond to motions, but I would suggest that that time be 14 days, Mr Wladimiroff, just as I gave 14 days at our last meeting to respond to what I think is going to be a motion filed by the Prosecutor, of course with leave to ask for additional time. So the first kind of ground rule is that you can assume that you will have 14 days to file a written response, unless, of course, additional time is given. The second ground rule is that oral hearings will be set for all motions. Perhaps, in this case, we will receive some routine motions, or requests, and of course if they are very routine, then maybe we can dispense with the need for a hearing. However, given the nature of the matter that we are considering, I would expect oral hearings will be held for all motions. Since we will be setting, then, an oral hearing for most motions, I would want to know from counsel an estimated time that they would need for this oral hearing so that if, for example, when we begin to hear from the Prosecutor with respect to the motions, or motion, that he intends on filing, I will ask you, Mr Niemann, if you can give me an estimate of how much time is needed. This will be true for all of the motions that we talk about. The other matter relating to motions is that, if either counsel wishes to have a consideration of the motion in camera, then you should tell me that today as well. Finally, the Tribunal, or I guess the Registry, actually, has issued a Manual for Practitioners, which you should have received. Have you, Mr Wladimiroff? PROFESSOR WLADIMIROFF: Yes, your Honour, we did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Let me remind you that that manual requires that an order, I do believe, a proposed order be submitted with all of the motions. In any case, you should be familiar with that manual. The Registry has made, I think, a very good effort to assist counsel, and understand our procedures. In addition to the pre-trial and preliminary motions that we may talk about today, I also want to talk about some general matters, for example, the handling of transcript corrections. Each of you should have received a transcript, and I think you need to know the Judges' views on how transcript corrections will be handled. The other matter is that I need to talk about the number of counsel that will be allowed for each side and the role of assistants. As I said, this is really a working session. We are really handling kind of mundane matters and not very interesting matters, I would suppose, to some people, except we all as lawyers and judges enjoy this very much, do we not? So, if there are any other matters that anyone wishes to raise today, we will attempt to consider that. I hope that we can consider all of these preliminary matters by 1.00. Is that not so? We will then stand in recess by 1.00. So we have plenty of time. Let us begin first with you, Mr Niemann. You indicated at the initial appearance that you wished to file a motion under Rule 69, was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Under Rule 75 primarily, your Honour. This will be a motion which we anticipate being able to file by the 18th May as I previously indicated, and it will deal with the issues of witnesses giving evidence before the Tribunal, those witnesses who are concerned for their safety in other matters. Your Honour, there is one issue that perhaps I might raise, while I am on my feet, in relation to this motion, with respect to one of the witnesses that we will be dealing with in the course of our motion. This relates to the first count in the Indictment, a count which is now numbered 4.1, and referred to in that count is the letter 'F'. This witness at the moment says she cannot bring herself to give evidence before the Tribunal, and I think it is incumbent upon me to say that, if she does not testify, or if her evidence is not admitted, the prospect of the prosecution proceeding with this count at this stage looks doubtful. So, your Honour, there is a possibility that, even if we proceed with the motion under 75, in relation to her specifically, even if orders sought were obtained, she may still refuse to give evidence. We are conscious of the need to ensure that we do not request the Tribunal to embark upon some hypothetical hearing, but the motion that we will be filing on 18th May will not only deal with her, but will deal with other witnesses as well. Our purpose in wanting to deal with this particular witness, in relation to this count, is that we feel that if we are successful in obtaining orders in the nature of those provided for under Rule 75(2) we will then at least have something concrete to go to the witness with to see whether or not she will be able to come forward under those circumstances to give evidence. But I thought it appropriate, your Honour, that we raise this at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: If I understand your motion, your motion then -- of course we will see it on the 18th -- will be directed towards this person who is referred to as 'F' in 4.1. It will refer to other potential witnesses and victims as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And other witnesses as well, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Will that motion require a public oral hearing, or will that have to be considered in camera?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We will be seeking that the hearing be heard in camera, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Do you know at this point how long you would need to present that motion approximately?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We estimate a day would be sufficient, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Is that all you want, one day? Of course that is your side. Do you anticipate any additional motions at this time?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Not at this stage, your Honour, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr Wladimiroff, you will be speaking now. Let me say again one preliminary matter. Mr Wladimiroff, as I indicated at the initial appearance, you have been designated as the lead attorney, so to speak, for Mr Tadic, and what that means is that we will ensure that all notices regarding any of the proceedings will be sent to you, and we will expect, in terms of arrangements, for you to notify other counsel of Mr Tadic. Mr Vujin was at the initial appearance, and we indicated that the Tribunal would attempt to send him notices as well, but we would look to you in terms of scheduling. Now, I see that we have been joined by another counsel, Mr Simic. Can you tell me what is his role, before you even tell me about your motions? PROFESSOR WLADIMIROFF: It does not change my position, as you described. Mr Simic is assisting Mr Vujin in what he is doing in Yugoslavia. For that reason, it does not change for your Court. You can still address me, and I will try to inform Mr Vujin that it is his duty to inform Mr Simic. There is no need for your Court to address Mr Simic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: That is helpful. So in terms of scheduling, again we will look to you and we will attempt to accommodate Mr Vujin, if we are able to. Then Mr Simic, of course, would be assisting Mr Vujin. Then no notices will be sent to Mr Simic. PROFESSOR WLADIMIROFF: That will not be necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Okay. Tell me, if you know at this point, what preliminary motions you intend to be filing, and pre-trial motions? PROFESSOR WLADIMIROFF: Yes, your Honour. If it may please your Court, we are intending to file a motion to dispute the jurisdiction of the Tribunal in the case of Mr Tadic, and this motion will be filed on Friday, June 23rd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: By when? June 23rd? PROFESSOR WLADIMIROFF: That is right. On that day, we will also file a motion that will deal with the principle of non-bis-in-idem. That is, in our opinion, the present prosecution of Mr Tadic is not consistent with Article 10 of the Statute. These are the two main motions. I think it is not necessary to say that of course we do regret that it will not be possible to file this motion on an earlier date, but your Honour will certainly appreciate that we are dealing with very complicated matters, areas of the law, that have been debated by experts for years, and I take it the Court will understand that we really do need the full period of 60 days. Beside these two motions, we intend to file a motion to exclude any evidence obtained from Mr Tadic by the German authorities, if we are not able to come to an agreement with the Prosecutor's Office on this matter. For that purpose, I will contact the Prosecutor's Office next week, and I do hope it will be successful to reach agreement on this matter. If not, we will file this motion on Friday, June 9th. Last, but not least, we have a motion in consideration about the form of the Indictment, but we have not yet decided on this issue. If we will file such a motion, it will be done together with the other two on June 23rd. Pre-trial motions, let me just see. It may be the case that, dependent on how things develop in Yugoslavia, it may be necessary that we have to file a motion as specified in Rule 71 to have depositions taken over there. We are not yet sure it will be necessary, but that problem may arise at a later stage. I hope to inform you as soon as we are convinced that it will be necessary, and then we can inform you about persons and more specific details about this matter. Those are the motions we are going to file or have in consideration or may have to file. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I understand it is difficult, and I do not expect you to give me a definitive list, just give us some guidance. The motion regarding non-bis-in-idem, when would you be filing that, Mr Wladimiroff? You may have said, but I missed it. PROFESSOR WLADIMIROFF: Sorry, on June 23rd, together with the jurisdiction matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: And possibly the motion regarding the form of the Indictment on the 23rd. The other motion regarding evidence would be filed, you expect, on June 9th; is that correct? PROFESSOR WLADIMIROFF: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Will all of these motions be presented in public, or is there a need to consider any of them in camera? PROFESSOR WLADIMIROFF: Maybe the pre-trial motion about taking this deposition might be in chambers, but I am not able to decide on that matter either. I am not sure what we will do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Do you know approximately how much time you might need for your presentation of these motions? PROFESSOR WLADIMIROFF: As they are filed on one day, I think it depends on whether your Court will deal with them on the same day. If you are going to deal with them on one day and not each motion separately, then provided you will deal with them on one day, I also will need one day, perhaps half a day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Our preference would be -- and we have talked about this before -- to hear as many motions, obviously, in one day, that we can. I do not know whether the motion regarding the jurisdiction of the Tribunal may take a little bit longer to hear than the other two, but we will schedule one day optimistically, but we might need two days, at least to hear from you and of course from the Prosecutor as well. The Prosecutor wants an entire day on his Rule 75 motion, which is okay. I think we will probably need three days to do your two motions that you will filing on the 23rd. PROFESSOR WLADIMIROFF: The presentation will not be that extensive, because we will try to put everything in the motion itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: That is helpful. It is certainly helpful to me to have as full a motion and brief, supporting the motion, and of course we will read it very carefully beforehand and so it will just be a question of asking you questions about it. You, of course, may want to summarise the motion, but we will be enquiring about the questions that we may have. Mr Niemann, were you thinking that maybe you would not need a day? Is that what you were thinking?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it depends on whether we proceed by way of affidavit or whether we proceed by way of having to call evidence. If we have to call some evidence, it may take longer. That is why I suggested a day, but it could be much shorter than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr Wladimiroff, of course you have not seen the motion that the Prosecutor is filing on the 18th. We have given you until June 2nd, as I recall, to respond, with leave to ask for additional time. In terms of scheduling of the hearing ---- PROFESSOR WLADIMIROFF: I take it, your Honour, that these 14 days will be sufficient now I have heard what the motion will be about. So it is very unlikely we will ask for an extension. Nevertheless, formally speaking, I think we have to reserve our rights for this extension. It is very unlikely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Excuse me, please. (Pause). We are trying to develop our procedures, and excuse me if we are proceeding slowly. It is really a question of how the Prosecutor would provide your motion to counsel for the defence, and that is how it is done at least in my system. What is wonderful is we come from all different systems and we are trying to create a system that is acceptable to all. We are doing pretty good thus far. Anyway, you would file your motion, Mr Niemann, nd of course you have indicated that there may be some affidavits. The hearing of this motion will be in camera, so I am sure that there would be attachments, and maybe even the motion itself would have to be under seal. Is that not so?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It seems so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: The question that was raised by the Deputy Registrar was how would that motion then be served on counsel for the accused. I would typically suggest that the motion be filed here, with the Registry, look at our Manual for the Practitioners and then you would send a copy of a typical motion indicating the certificate of service, on counsel for the accused. Of course, this motion that you are filing is rather sensitive, I suppose, in nature. How did you anticipate handling that? That is assuming that counsel for the accused was in a position to respond to that motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would your Honour excuse me for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Yes. (Pause). Yes, Mr Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have just had a discussion with my colleague. We believe that we can file it. We will not be making any request that the motion itself or the affidavits in support will have any need for confidentiality of those, or non-publication of those. We are not concerned about that. I think we will file in the ordinary way and have it served in the ordinary way. The issues that are likely to arise during the oral presentation of the information we would expect touch on are matters that we would at least prefer a hearing in camera for. The motion and declarations in support, they need not be kept confidential.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: What Mr Marro has suggested, the Deputy Registrar, is that you then file this motion along with any attachments that you may have, and may I suggest that, in addition to the affidavits, you give us a brief, some statement of authority? If it is nothing more than referring us to the Statute of the Tribunal and to our Rules, whatever authorities you may feel are appropriate, because we are borrowing now from other international, perhaps, authorities. You file that with the Registry. The Registry has told me that they will then send certified copies to counsel for the accused. They would be able to do that in that day. That is provided that you do not file them at 5.00 on May 18th, but certainly if it were that late, then by the next day they will then issue certified copies -- is that correct, Mr Marro -- to counsel for the accused. I do not mean to overstate what you have told me. Is that correct? Then file them with the Registry and then the Registry will prepare certified copies, and then those will be served on counsel for the accused. The time, then, for you to respond to those motions again would be 14 days from the time that you receive them, because who knows what might happen. I would not expect that there will be a significant delay. Your time to respond begins from the date that you receive them. PROFESSOR WLADIMIROFF: We are aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Very good. That is something accomplished. Regarding the hearing on that motion, which you have indicated might take a day, Mr Niemann, you are probably speaking from your side, so we might need even a little bit longer. We will set a hearing on the motion that the Prosecutor will be filing pursuant to Rule 75 of our Rules for Wednesday, June 21st at 10.00 am. We will reserve additional time, perhaps even going into Thursday, 22nd, if necessary. This is not to encourage anyone to spend additional time, but if you need it, we will set aside two days starting at 10.00. That will then be in camera. With respect to the motions that Mr Wladimiroff has indicated that he intends on filing, Mr Niemann, one is the motion to dispute the jurisdiction of the Tribunal, non-bis-in-idem, and the form of the indictment. These he intends to file by June 23rd, and perhaps may file another motion by June 9th, regarding the exclusion of evidence obtained by the German authorities. Again, without seeing the motions, we will give you 14 days to respond to those motions. If you need additional time, then request it from the Court. I am sure that you have done some enquiry on these issues, and so although you have not received the motion itself, you are probably in a good position to respond, even without seeing the motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: In any case, 14 days to respond to each of the motions that counsel for the accused has indicated that he will be filing, and Mr Wladimiroff, again, you would then file those motions, with supporting authorities, with the Registry. The Registry would then prepare certified copies, and then send those copies to the Office of the Prosecutor, which will not be a difficult task, since they are in the same building somewhere. Let me see if I can set some dates. (Pause). The motions, Mr Wladimiroff, you have indicated that you were going to file by June 23rd, and then of course the Prosecutor will have 14 days to respond, unless you need additional time. We will set an oral hearing for those motions on July 25th, and we will reserve an additional two days. So we can plan that we will begin on July 25th, at 10.00 am, and there is, of course, no indication, there has been no request, and you can see no need to have those in camera. So we will then proceed at 10.00, July 25th. We will reserve the 26th and 27th, if necessary, so that we can hear arguments on all the motions. If we can finish, of course, in two days, then we would be happy to. With respect to the other motion that you have indicated that you would file, Mr Wladimiroff, the motion possibly to exclude evidence obtained by German authorities that you are filing on June 9th, you anticipate? PROFESSOR WLADIMIROFF: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr Niemann, Judge Deschênes would like to address some matter to you regarding this June 9th motion, this motion that Mr Wladimiroff indicates that he will file on June 9th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DESCHENES
utterances.text: It is purely a mechanical concern. I was wondering whether you would be prepared to show some flexibility with respect to the delays. Mr Wladimiroff has announced his motion for the 9th. We also know that we will be proceeding on your own motion on the 21st.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DESCHÊNES
utterances.text: And possibly on the 22nd if it just flows over. Would you be prepared to proceed on the same occasion on the Defence motion that has been announced for exclusion of evidence coming from the German authorities? I am asking you that, because this would give you slightly less than the formal 14 days of delay, and that is why I was talking about some possible flexibility on your part.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am sure we could attempt to combat that. If there is a problem, we will raise it. Other than that, we are very happy for that to be set at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DESCHÊNES
utterances.text: So we could maybe foresee that the Defence motion could be set for, say, the 22nd, for instance?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DESCHÊNES
utterances.text: If Madam President agrees with that. I do not know if Mr Wladimiroff feels that that can be arranged. PROFESSOR WLADIMIROFF: I think that can be arranged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: If we gave you your 14 days, and we are now talking of 14 calendar days, you would have until the 23rd. Is that right, with my addition?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That looks right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: What we are asking is if you file it earlier and then we combine the hearing. The hearing on your motion is scheduled for the 21st, with the possible overflow to the 22nd. If we are to hear the motion that Mr Wladimiroff is filing on June 9th, we would need a response from you earlier, even before the 21st, so that we will have a chance to look at it and be a little informed. May I ask you to file your response by June 19th? That is taking away four days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. We will endeavour to meet that date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: If you are not able to do it, let us know and we will see if we can reschedule it. If you can do that -- I am just taking away four days -- we will receive your response by June 19th to the motion regarding exclusion of evidence obtained by German authorities, that Mr Wladimiroff will be filing on June 9th. Again, file it with the Registry. The Registry then will quickly certify that motion and get it quickly to Mr Wladimiroff, probably by hand delivery, so that he is able to take a look at the response and then be prepared ---- PROFESSOR WLADIMIROFF: I suppose it has to be handed over to the Prosecutor, because we filed that motion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Pardon me? PROFESSOR WLADIMIROFF: You indicated it will be handed over to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I mean his response. The response that he is going to file on June 19th will be handed over to you, so that you quickly, the same day, will have a chance to take a look at it. When we hear it on the 21st, late, or perhaps on the 22nd, depending upon our time, you will have had a chance to look at it. The only possible motion that we have not considered, in terms of just scheduling, is the one that Mr Wladimiroff has indicated that he may file pursuant to Rule 71. If you file it, Mr Wladimiroff, just indicate in the submission papers that you file with the Registry whether there is a need to have that in camera, and also indicate, if you are able to, just an estimate of the time that would be needed to present an oral argument on that motion. PROFESSOR WLADIMIROFF: We will do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Are there any other matters that we need to consider regarding the filing of motions, either preliminary motions or pre-trial motions?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this may amount to a motion ultimately, but with the issue of discovering material, we have already discovered the material under Rule 66(A) on 26th April 1995, but I would like to indicate that more material is coming to hand, almost on a daily basis, and we will progressively discover this to the defence following our assessment of the material and our determination that we will seek, or want to use it during the course of the proceedings. I raise this at this stage because it occurs to us that it may give rise, possibly, to an amendment to the Indictment, but no decision has been made on that yet. I think it is proper that I should foreshadow the possibility of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr Wladimiroff, Mr Niemann has indicated that he considers that he has complied with Rule 66(A), and that is to provide, as soon as practicable after the initial appearance of the accused, copies of the supporting material which accompanied the Indictment, when the confirmation was sought. Have you been provided with the accompanying material? PROFESSOR WLADIMIROFF: We have, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps your Honour, for the record, I should indicate that we have given Mr Wladimiroff everything other than that material that will be affected by our Rule 75 application. PROFESSOR WLADIMIROFF: That is what we understood, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Of course, for any other reciprocal discovery, or any discovery that you may wish to request, Mr Wladimiroff, under Rule 66(B) that is of course up to you at the appropriate day. PROFESSOR WLADIMIROFF: Yes. Of course we do realise we have to disclose to the Prosecutor on our side too. That will be a bit later. I hope you will understand this is due to work we have to accomplish these days. We will take care that we will do this in due time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: If you request items under 66(B), then that kind of triggers, I guess, the reciprocal discovery. I do not know if you are even going to request things under 66(B). PROFESSOR WLADIMIROFF: It is not very likely, but we will take care of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Okay. Are there other matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps, your Honour, I might indicate that it is our intention to proceed by making everything available to Mr Wladimiroff that we possibly can, as soon as we can. Whether or not he makes a formal request under 66(B) or not, that will not affect the approach we wish to take in this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: So you will kind of have an open file, or that is too broad a statement, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is not an open file, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: You will endeavour to provide him with matters that may even go beyond 66(A), that is what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Is there anything else now with respect to either preliminary motions or pre-trial motions? PROFESSOR WLADIMIROFF: No, your Honour, we have no other things to discuss on this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: There are a few matters I have been asked to talk about today, I suppose. The first relates to the release of audiovisual transmission. I have been signing an order routinely at the start of each of the proceedings that we have had in this matter that authorises the release of the audiovisual transcription -- not the transcription. It gets a bit difficult when I start to talk about technical matters, and the lights too are dimming, are they not? What it means is it goes out to the press automatically. I have been signing that order, because that is the procedure that we have followed. That is whatever our director films is released to the press. I want you to be aware of that. It is a standard order that is signed by the Tribunal. Miss Hollis, I see you may have a question. Do you have a question regarding that?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: If I may confer with Mr Niemann.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just in respect of that, we certainly have no problem with the proceedings being sent out to the public. Our only concern is likely to arise -- and I think it is proper I should mention it now -- during the course of trial, with witnesses. In respect of some witnesses, not all, but some witnesses we feel it would be very detrimental if their faces were exposed throughout the world in the course of them giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Yes. Mr Wladimiroff? PROFESSOR WLADIMIROFF: Your Honour, I think we will support that idea. Also on our side we may present witnesses who are not very fond of being exposed. So for the same reasons, we will support that idea, not to have them in the public, with their faces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: First of all, Rule 75 of our Rules permit protection of victims and witnesses through a number of procedures, but we certainly are aware of that, and will abide by the request of counsel. That can be handled simply by asking the person who is responsible for the video for the Tribunal not to video or focus in on the witnesses. The Tribunal, or at least the Judges, are in the process of preparing some guidelines for ourselves, just to make sure that we have sufficient control over that, and so I am sensitive to it, and we will abide by your request. We will take care of that when it occurs, but we are very sensitive to that and will respect your wishes. The other standard matter is that still photographers appear at the start of each of our sessions. You may or may not have noticed them. I see you smiling, Mr Fenrick, I kind of have the same feeling. They come in and they are only allowed a short time, and they take still photographs. That is an order that again I simply sign routinely. I want you to be aware of that, if there is a problem. PROFESSOR WLADIMIROFF: We have no problem with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We do not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you. The other problem I was supposed to raise -- and I was concerned, I suppose, and it may come a little late -- is to speak slowly, because sometimes the interpreter needs additional time. Let us try to speak slowly, if we can. We want to -- as when I began the proceedings -- make sure that everyone is able to hear the translation, or interpretation, rather, through their earphones. For this trial, and all of the preliminary matters that we will consider before the actual commencement of the trial, there will be only an English transcript, and the English transcript is prepared, and remarkably so, simultaneously. There will be a French translation, but not a French transcript that is prepared. So what you will receive is the English transcript, and there will at the appropriate time be a French translation. Is that acceptable? The handling of transcript corrections. Let me share with you the procedure that we follow. We receive the transcript and then each of the Judges reviews it to determine whether they consider there are any errors, and then of course counsel is given the transcript and they then are permitted to at least advise the Tribunal of any errors that they consider exist with respect to the transcription. Then I would be certainly willing, and have then directed that the transcript be modified to reflect those corrections, but we will not have any stylistic changes. For example, most often when I read a transcript of things that I have said, I would prefer to have said them differently sometimes, a little more eloquently and more artfully, but I do not have that opportunity to make that change on a transcript and counsel will not either. So it is just typographical errors. We saw some the last time. There was a word, for example, Mr Niemann I think the transcript read "released" and it should have been something else, I forget what. "Arrests", I think. That was changed, because upon review we determined that you had actually said "arrests", and so we changed it to that. Is that acceptable?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. PROFESSOR WLADIMIROFF: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: We do have space limitations. Typically, only counsel would be permitted to sit at counsel table, but we will allow non- lawyers who are serving as your legal assistants to be at counsel table, Mr Wladimiroff. There has to be a limitation, and as you will notice, both tables, both for the prosecution and for the defence, only have six spaces. So I do not know how it can be handled other than you have six seats. You may fill them as you wish. PROFESSOR WLADIMIROFF: That will not be a problem for us. It is more a matter of practical reasons, when the real trial starts, I want those people beside me who handle the parts of the trial. I can arrange that. It is a matter of scheduling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: That is acceptable. There may be different assistants. For example, this gentleman here, whose name I thought I did not have to remember, may be here for some witnesses, and then of course another one may be available for another witness. PROFESSOR WLADIMIROFF: That is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: You have a defence room, and that is acceptable. He can go and you can bring in another. We only have room for six. Of course, since they are not attorneys, they will not, then, be wearing robes and they would not address the Court, but they are here to assist you. That is acceptable to me. Anything from the Office of the Prosecutor by way of preliminary matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am not sure whether it is preliminary, your Honour, but the one issue we would like to raise that goes to the question of the organisation of our potential witnesses when the trial starts, I wonder, will the Chamber be recessing for the summer break and is it likely that the trial will then be after that? I wonder that, because it does assist us when dealing with our witnesses. Witnesses ring us and they ask, "When are we likely to be expected?" and so forth, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: What is the summer recess?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I question whether there is one or not. I heard some rumour that there was to be one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: At the present time, I do not know that we have firmly decided this matter. Certainly in terms of a recess, as I indicated at the initial appearance, Mr Tadic has been in custody for a while. It is nearly over a year now. I guess an adjournment, at least so far as the German authorities are concerned -- I am sure that everyone is anxious to have the trial begin as quickly as possible, and we will work with you to accomplish that. There are jurisdictional motions, though, that you have indicated that you intend on filing, Mr Wladimiroff, and just as a matter of practicality, depending upon how we rule on those motions, there may be an appeal taken. Either side, as you know, under our Rules, may have an interlocutory appeal on this preliminary motion that is dealing with the jurisdiction of the Court so that, when you file your motion on June 23rd, then the Prosecutor will respond, and we have set our date for a hearing of that motion that will be in late July. We would have to rule on that motion, and if there is an appeal taken, then of course you would have to look at our Rules to see how much time is given -- 30 days, I believe -- to file your briefs, et cetera. So if this matter is still in this Trial Chamber, we want to try it obviously as quickly as possible. If, because of any jurisdictional motions and our ruling of those jurisdictional motions, if there is an appeal taken, it is out of our hands. That would have to be handled by the Appeals Chamber. Depending upon how they rule, there would be a trial, or there would not be a trial, if they agreed with your motion. So the answer to your question is that it probably will kind of play itself out because of the jurisdictional motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I understand, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Are there any other matters? This is your last opportunity today. If anything occurs to you that you wish to bring to the attention of the Chamber by way of a pre-trial matter or preliminary matter, please feel free to contact us in writing by submitting that to the Registry, and they will, of course, get that to the Judges. If there is nothing else, then, the Chamber will adjourn until June 21st at 10.00 am. Thank you.
